title: The classroom at Nicopolis
hook: the Discourses are a student's notes of Epictetus teaching young men

segments.voice: Yesterday: enchiridion, the handbook, fifty-three sections closed and three kept in the hand. Your line was carry three. Which three did you choose? Day three hundred eighty-eight.

Northwest Greece, under the Roman emperors. A city by the sea with a name that means victory city. In a room somewhere in it, a teacher who was once enslaved is talking to a class of young men. He teases them. He loses patience with them. He tells them stories about their own vanity until they squirm. And in the room is a student writing down every word he can catch. Today a new part of the path begins. Today: the classroom at Nicopolis.
screen: `A CITY CALLED VICTORY.` → `A TEACHER, ONCE ENSLAVED.` → `THE CLASSROOM AT NICOPOLIS.`

segments.voice: First, the teacher. Epictetus was enslaved in Rome. Ancient writers name his owner: Epaphroditus, himself a freedman who had served Nero. Epictetus studied philosophy with the Stoic Musonius Rufus, and at some point was freed. Then, the writer Aulus Gellius reports, the emperor Domitian expelled the philosophers from Rome, and Epictetus moved across the sea to Nicopolis. Second, the city. Nicopolis, victory city, was where he opened a school, and young men came to hear him. Third, the notes. One of those students was Arrian, who later wrote a history of Alexander the Great. Arrian wrote down what he heard. In a short letter at the front of the Discourses, he says he didn't compose them like a book. He tried to record his teacher's words as nearly as he could in the very words used, as reminders of his thinking and his frankness. That's why they sound like speech, full of questions and jokes and rough corners. Fourth, what changes for us. The handbook was the summary. The Discourses are the classroom. You'll hear Epictetus interrupt, argue with imaginary students, mock the proud and lose patience with the lazy. It's the difference between reading a recipe and standing in the kitchen. For the next weeks, we're in the kitchen. A real classroom.
screen: `FROM ENSLAVED TO TEACHER.` · `NICOPOLIS: VICTORY CITY.` · `ARRIAN WROTE DOWN THE VERY WORDS.` · `THE HANDBOOK SUMMARIZED; THIS IS THE ROOM.` · then, large: `A REAL CLASSROOM.`

segments.voice: If you have a book nearby, any book that matters to you, open it to one paragraph. If not, recall one section of the handbook you chose yesterday. Read it, or say it, out loud, slowly, the way it might have sounded in a classroom by the sea. Listen to your own voice saying it. Notice what you hear that you missed reading silently. Then rest in the quiet after the words. The bell holds the time.
Arrian. The student who wrote down his teacher's words as nearly as he could, at the school in Nicopolis. Today's word.
Your line: a real classroom. Read one paragraph aloud today, from any book that matters to you, as if you were in that room. Day three hundred eighty-eight.

howItsDone: Some readers of the Discourses read passages aloud, since Arrian says he tried to keep his teacher's spoken words rather than write a polished book.

original.note: Greek: victory city, from nikē, victory, and polis, city; Epictetus' home and school.

trapdoor: what you thought: an old philosophy book.
what it means: a student's notes of a former slave teaching young men, kept as close to his spoken words as possible.
what a scholar hears: Arrian's preface to Lucius Gellius, which says he kept his teacher's very words as reminders of his thought and frankness.
recall: the ruling part of the mind

notes: Biography: born at Hierapolis in Phrygia (c. 50–55 CE); enslaved in Rome, owned by Epaphroditus (freedman and secretary of Nero); studied with Musonius Rufus; freed; Domitian's expulsion of philosophers (c. 89 or 93–95 CE); school at Nicopolis in Epirus. Confirm dates and phrasing.
Nicopolis founded by Octavian/Augustus to commemorate Actium (31 BCE). Confirm.
Arrian of Nicomedia: later consul (c. 130 CE) and historian of Alexander (Anabasis). Confirm.
Arrian's preface: he did not compose the discourses as literature, but tried to write down what he heard in the very words, as memorials of Epictetus' thought and frankness. Paraphrased; confirm.
Four books survive; Photius refers to eight, and Aulus Gellius cites a fifth. 'Ancient writers mention more' stated generally; confirm.

Editor review (2026-10-01): cut dates and claims not in the cited sources (year one hundred, rich students from Rome, Phrygia, founding by Augustus at Actium, consulship, 'four books survive, more lost', 'everyday Greek'); tied Domitian's expulsion and the move to Nicopolis to Aulus Gellius; Epaphroditus now introduced as named by ancient writers, with the Discourses passages added as a source; replaced the myth item on lost books and the unsourced howItsDone claim.
